opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to where knowledge actually lives. If you look at how humans and animals come to understand the world, very little of it comes from language. A baby learns that objects persist when they go behind something, that unsupported things fall, that pushing something makes it move, long before they have words for any of that. That understanding is grounded in what they see, hear, and touch, and in how those signals change over time and in response to their own actions.

Text is incredibly useful, but it's a compressed, filtered description of the world written by people who already understand it. A lot of the most basic physical and causal structure is never written down because it's so obvious to us. So if you want a system that has that kind of common-sense model of how the world works, how things move, interact, and respond to interventions, you have to give it access to the signal where that structure is actually present, which is the sensory stream itself, video especially.

The other piece is scale and self-supervision. There's an enormous amount of perceptual data out there, and it doesn't need labels. The world itself provides the supervision: if you can predict what happens next, or fill in what's missing, you've learned something real about its structure. The trick, and a lot of what we've worked on with joint-embedding predictive architectures like I-JEPA and V-JEPA, is to do that prediction in a learned representation space rather than at the pixel level. You don't want the model wasting capacity predicting every leaf flickering in the background; you want it capturing the things that are predictable and matter, like where an object is going or what an agent is about to do.

And ultimately that's what lets you go beyond recognition toward planning. If a model has learned from observation how the world evolves, you can condition it on actions and use it as a world model, imagining the consequences of what you might do before you do it. That's a capability I think is really hard to get purely from language, and it's essential if we want systems, robots in particular, that can act sensibly in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response says that understanding is grounded in what humans and animals see, hear, and touch, and that systems need access to sensory signals to build a model of how the world works.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the way I think about it is, if you look at how humans and animals come to understand the world, we're not learning from labels or from text. An infant, in the first few months of life, builds up a surprisingly rich model of how objects behave, that things persist when they're occluded, that they fall when unsupported, just by watching and interacting. And all of that comes from raw sensory input, mostly vision.

So perceptual signals like video are, in some sense, the most direct window we have into the structure of the physical world. Language is incredibly powerful, but it's a compressed, human-curated description of the world. It tells you what someone chose to say about a scene, not what's actually in it. If you want a system that has intuitive physics, that understands space, motion, cause and effect at a grounded level, I think you have to learn that from the signal itself, because text just doesn't contain most of that information. Nobody writes down that a cup sitting on a table doesn't float away.

The other piece is scale and supervision. There's an essentially unlimited amount of video and sensory data out there, and it doesn't require anyone to annotate it. If we can get learning algorithms that extract useful abstractions from that data on their own, the way self-supervised learning did for language, that's the path toward world models that can actually support planning and reasoning about physical outcomes, not just pattern matching on what's been described before.

And a point I'd emphasize is that this doesn't mean predicting every pixel. A lot of what's in a video is irrelevant detail, the exact texture of leaves moving in the wind. What we care about is learning representations where the predictable, semantically meaningful structure is captured and the noise is abstracted away. That's really the motivation behind the work we've been doing with JEPA-style architectures, learning to predict in representation space rather than in input space. The goal is a model that understands the world well enough to anticipate what will happen next, and I think perceptual data is the only place that understanding can come from.

r001.rationale: The candidate says perceptual signals provide a direct window into the physical world and that learning from them is needed for grounded understanding of space, motion, and cause and effect.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of what we understand about the world is hard to express in language. If you watch an object fall or see someone interact with something, you pick up information about motion, space, and cause and effect that might never be explicitly described. Language captures some of that, but it’s already an abstraction of the underlying experience.

So if we want models to understand the world, learning directly from perceptual signals seems like an important piece. They need to discover structure in what they observe—what changes, what stays the same, and what might happen next. The hope is that those representations can then support things like prediction and planning, rather than requiring us to spell out everything about the world in words.

r001.rationale: The response says models need to learn from what they observe to understand the world, grounding that learning in perceptual information such as motion, space, and cause and effect.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of what we know about the world is difficult to put into words. If you watch an object fall, or watch someone interact with something, there’s a tremendous amount of information in that observation. You learn about motion, physical constraints, and how things relate to each other without anyone having to describe those relationships to you.

Language gives us a really powerful way to communicate and organize knowledge, but it’s also a compressed description of our experience. Learning directly from perceptual signals gives a model access to some of the information that never makes it into that description. The challenge is figuring out what to learn from those signals—what’s useful for understanding and predicting the world, rather than just capturing every detail of an image.

r001.rationale: The response says perceptual signals let a model learn about motion, physical constraints, and relationships directly from observation, giving it information needed to understand the world.
